commentBody: What's a penny?

In yesterday’s comments @Lm asked me for a response that I didn’t see until late, and I think it’s such a legitimate question that it deserves an answer. They essentially asked for some specifics about what made yesterday’s puzzle easier for a Saturday, and how anyone could call this “a Tuesday puzzle”.

The answer is, no thoughtful commentator would call it a Tuesday puzzle, but they might complain about too many Tuesday clues spoiling the solve. And it doesn’t necessarily take a lot. For yesterday, 1-d was “Into every life, some ___ must fall—Longfellow.” In my opinion, that’s a Tuesday clue. It’s an extremely common phrase and even if you’ve never heard it, it’s extremely guessable. But more importantly it’s 1-D. So you’ve basically spent so much time laboring over a beautiful set of four long stacked entries, and handed me, for free, the first letter of each of them. It’s a huge leg up and the equivalent, to use Anonymous’s analogy, of putting bumpers on an experienced bowler’s lane. And it seems so unnecessary—we’re not asking to change the grid, just give us a more puzzling clue.
Anyway, that’s my take, and I hope no one considers it elitism or boasting, just an honest response to a fair question.

Wondering if anyone else did a double take at the clueing of HAREM and questioned whether it was culturally tone-deaf.

I’m trying to keep an open mind about it. Reading more about it, I understand it was a place where women could interact with each other in a safe, secluded place and that it was a respected family institution. But on the other hand, in the bigger picture, it seems like it was an institutionalized way to keep women from interacting with the outside world, and the fact that it was thought of as “protection” gives some indication of their status—who or what did they need “protecting” from?

So, ultimately, it just seemed like a clue that seems to promote a positive connotation on a cultural practice which doesn’t seem at all positive from our modern perspective. To use an extreme example, if there were a clue for some protected space for slaves in America, I doubt that would be well-received. Maybe that’s a stretch and I hope not offensive to anyone. Just wondering if it gave anyone else pause.

117A  [Tree where the Buddha found enlightenment]

I read about the BODHI tree when I was 20 and read the great historical book "SIDDHARTHA" by Hermann Hesse about the life of Buddha. 

Well, Buddha was a real person, just like Jesus. He had a very rich life and at the end of it (spoiler alert, LOL) he found solace sitting under the BODHI tree and watching the river go by. The river is a metaphor for life as it is constantly changing and it is difficult to say what the river really is: it has many forms. This is reminiscent of the yin/yang of life where the light has some dark in it and the dark has some light in it (and it's all always changing) and it's all part of a unified whole.

This story reminds me of Shel Silverstein's book "The Giving Tree" mentioned here yesterday where our hero finds the same comfort resting on an old stump at the end of his life.

I do too. I had a beautiful old mulberry tree in my backyard. The cacophony of the birds when the tree was full of fruit...the fruit itself...and the fallen leaves enriched my garden soil. The tree got too big and had to be cut down. The tree men cut several large sections of the trunk for me and they stand like sentinels in my yard. I sit on them and watch the bees and the flowers and the butterflies and soak up the sun. Who could ask for anything more?

To continue musing on a thread from yesterday: 

I finished the Saturday puzzle 26% faster than my recent average, but somehow it felt hard.
I finished today's puzzle 24% faster than my recent average, but it felt easy. (Though delightful.)

XWStats has both currently rated Average (yes, yesterday's rating is back up to Average again), with the median solver who reports there solving each of them 16% faster than their recent times. 

I'm endlessly fascinated by subjective experience. What makes a puzzle feel satisfying? I think perhaps, for me, the most important thing is to have at least one point in the solve where I don't think I'm going to be able to finish, a point where I have to sit back and rethink my strategies to complete it. Accomplishing that, for me, is much more satisfying than rapid rote recall. I don't want to learn just new facts, but new strategies.

Wondering how much this differs depending on where in our learning curves we are. And in what era we began solving.

So, the American Coinage Act of 1792 stipulates four different denominations: dollars, dismes [sic], cents (i.e. pennies), and mils. Now, mils have never existed as real coinage--they exist only in property taxes and gas stations--and no 1 mil. coins were ever minted, although some states did produce mil "tokens," as a means to pay local sales taxes. But there were half-cent pieces (which were effectively 5 mils), minted 1793-1857. (Although I'm not sure they were ever called "ha'pennies.") When they were finally phased out, they had a purchasing power equivalent to about $.12 in 2026 dollars.

This is from someone who has zero experience as a sound professional, but has been around for more than 25 years. 

“Microphone” was originally shortened to “mike” because of normal English spelling conventions. And it was spelled that way everywhere it appeared. 

Then, as gear became smaller and lighter, there wasn’t enough room on amp(lifier)s and stereo(phonic record player)s and the like, so the first three letters appeared on the inputs, along with the VOL(Ume) knob and other shortenings. 

People started using the written abbrev. for the spoken shortening, even though the labeling wasn’t meant to be spoken. (Much like the PED XING signs on street corners). 

Time passed, and like dials on phones and hands on clocks, a newer generation tripped over something that somehow got lost in the translation. Now, very few people remember that people regularly spelled it “mike.”  But they rage at that usage as if it were somehow ridiculous. 

But they did, and it still makes more sense.
